newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium's PM Dehaene backs scandal-hit minister.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's PM Dehaene backs scandal-hit minister.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene on Thursday backed his deputy Elio Di Rupo, alleged to have had sex with under-age boys, but was accused by the opposition of putting his government's survival above morals.

With the centre-left coalition government sitting on a powder keg, the Belgian parliament voted 103-20 in support of a special commission recommendation to continue enquiries into the charges which Di Rupo -- a discreet homosexual -- denies.
"In view of the state of the judicial procedure it would be premature at this stage to take a political decision and (Di Rupo) retains my confidence," Dehaene told parliament.
He added that Di Rupo, 45, had personally assured him the charges were baseless and that he could continue to carry out his ministerial duties.
The parliament said the enquiries into the allegations, which one member of the commission said were conflicting, had to be completed by December 9.

At the end of that period, with more information from the Brussels public prosecutor, the commission will decide whether to recommend parliament to lift Di Rupo's immunity and send him before the Cour de Cassation -- Belgium's highest court.

"For the minister, political leaders, the system of political democracy and the sense of justice of the whole population it is of the utmost importance to clarify this case as soon as possible," Dehaene said.
But the opposition immediately went on the offensive.

"My party believes Deputy Prime Minister Di Rupo has to step down...he no longer has the political integrity and moral authority required of a deputy prime minister," said Patrick Dewael, parliamentary leader of the Flemish Liberal Party.
If Di Rupo is sent to the court he will almost automatically be forced to resign. Even if the case is thrown out he has been politically weakened -- perhaps mortally wounded.
On Thursday Belgian newspapers questioned the reliability of the witness whose statements incriminated the minister.
But it is not only the fate of Di Rupo, a francophone socialist, that hangs in the balance.

The commission's decision was reached only after Dehaene pressured his own Christian Democratic Party to support Di Rupo. Belgium's coalition government consists of the francophone and Flemish christian democratic and socialist parties.
"This is the umpteenth proof that you and your party are being held hostage by the PS (the francophone socialist party)," Dewael said.
"You are afraid that Di Rupo's stepping down could spell the end of the government," he added, warning that public distrust and discontent would grow.
Rifts between the seven coalition representatives on the commission may translate into ruptures in the government itself.

The whole political and judicial establishment are already under fire for ineptitude and suspicions of corruption after the discovery of a paedophile abduction case and an unrelated political murder scandal three months ago.

The arrest in mid-August of convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux, the subsequent rescue of two sexually abused young girls from a house he owned and the discovery of the bodies of four more girls has shattered public confidence.

Last month 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels for a march that was intended to show support for the victims of sexual abuse and their parents but rapidly turned into a demonstration of disgust with what is seen as a corrupt system.
